t.2.59.1: Then, when the night had passed, early in the morning of the next day, the bards came and attended at that royal palace.
t.2.59.2: Then the attendants, pure in conduct and skilled in service, most of them women and eunuchs, waited upon him as before.
t.2.59.3: Those skilled in the art of bathing brought water mixed with yellow sandalwood in golden pitchers, at the proper time and according to rule.
t.2.59.4: Likewise other women, most of them young maidens, brought auspicious articles to be touched and provisions to be eaten.
t.2.59.5: Then those women who were nearest to the bed of the lord of the Kosalas came together and awakened their husband.
t.2.59.6: Seized with trembling and fearing for the king's life, they shook all over, like the tips of grass standing against the current of a stream.
t.2.59.7: Then, when the trembling women looked upon the king, the evil that had been feared became a certainty for them.
t.2.59.8: Then those noble women, stricken with grief, cried out loudly, like female elephants in the forest whose herd-leader has been driven from his place.
t.2.59.9: At the sound of their wailing, Kausalyā and Sumitrā suddenly came to their senses and woke from their sleep.
t.2.59.10: Kausalyā and Sumitrā, seeing the king and touching him, cried out, "Alas, O lord!" and fell upon the surface of the earth.
t.2.59.11: Writhing upon the ground, that daughter of the lord of Kosala, begrimed with dust, no longer shone, like a star fallen from the sky.
t.2.59.13: At once the palace of the king who had met his end became bereft of joy, wretched and distraught to behold.
t.2.59.12: That dwelling was terrified and bewildered, crowded with distraught people, filled on every side with tumultuous wailing, its kinsfolk stricken with grief.
t.2.59.14: Knowing that the illustrious bull among kings had passed away, his wives surrounded him and, weeping bitterly and piteously, deeply grief-stricken, they clasped his arms and lamented like women without a protector.
